In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of satellite retrievals of upper tropospherical ozone and nitric acids.
the evaluation and comparison of satellite retrievals of O3 and nitric acid with in situ observations.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ACE-FTS ozone is too high by 10–13% and that OSIRIS ozone is too high (5%), while both satellite instruments show a positive bias in nitric acid (ACE-FTs 15%; OSIRIS 10%).
the ozone and nitric oxide measurements of the two satellite instruments are in reasonable agreement with each other and with the in situ measurements, although the agreement is not perfect.
the satellite observations are in good agreement with the aircraft measurements, and that the GEOS-Chem model reproduces the observations well.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ACE‐FTS retrievals of ozone are generally reliable but have a positive bias of 13%.
the satellite measurements are useful for constraining the model simulations and that the satellite measurements can provide new insight into upper tropospheric chemistry.
satellite observations can provide valuable insight into ozone production efficiency in remote regions, where there are few in situ measurements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of satellite and in situ observations can help us better understand and quantify the processes controlling the abundance of tropospheric ozone.
satellite observations of upper tropospherically ozone and nitric oxide can be used to estimate upper limits on the upper tropospheric O3 production efficiency.
satellite measurements can provide useful constraints for ozone production in the upper tropopause.
